AAON_2017q3: AAON entered the August 2017 report off a weak first quarter — flat sales, earnings down 11.5% — but backlog jumped 40.9% to $68.9 million, shifting focus toward whether order recovery would show up in shipments. Coverage was thin, with no major catalysts beyond a routine dividend.
AAON_2018q4: AAON entered November 2018 with record demand but deteriorating profitability: Q2 sales rose 8.2% while net income fell 15.2%, even as backlog surged 87.5%. Management had already flagged the fix — pricing and better throughput — so investors were watching whether the causes looked temporary and demand stayed intact.
AAON_2019q2: AAON entered May 2019 mid-recovery: 2018 sales hit a record but margins had compressed on labor and material costs, with fixes underway. The stock had already run up sharply, so investors wanted proof price increases were finally offsetting costs and record backlog would convert into profitable, not just larger, volume.
AAON_2019q4: Heading into October 2019, the question was whether AAON could convert strong demand into shipments. The prior quarter had missed estimates, with management blaming sheet-metal equipment downtime, not weak orders. AAON ordered more fabrication machines and committed to a Texas expansion, underscoring capacity, not demand, as the constraint.
AAON_2020q1: AAON entered February 2020 still testing whether new fabrication capacity added in Q3 2019 would lift throughput and margins after a nearly flat quarter. The report landed the same day a coronavirus-driven selloff pushed the S&P 500 into correction, meaning any positive reaction had to reflect strong, company-specific news.
AAON_2020q2: The months before AAON's May 2020 report shifted the debate from execution to pandemic resilience, after a strong February quarter showed new equipment improving throughput. AAON rush-produced HVAC units for a temporary COVID hospital in New York, and saw an operations leadership transition as its longtime VP retired.
AAON_2021q4: AAON entered November 2021 with demand clearly outrunning its ability to produce profitably. Q2 sales hit a record with backlog up 33% and bookings up roughly 70%, so demand wasn't in question — margins were, on labor and material cost pressure. The stock also entered from a position of strength.
AAON_2022q3: AAON entered August 2022 with a damaged profitability story: an earlier earnings miss and market weakness had pressured shares, as inflation and low-priced backlog absorbed the benefit of strong revenue growth. Price increases and the BasX acquisition were underway, but much of the backlog still predated those price actions.
AAON_2023q1: AAON entered February 2023 with the debate shifting from whether pricing could catch inflation to how fast the company could convert its backlog at improved margins. A weak mid-2022 quarter had given way to improving efficiency. The stock hadn't run up sharply beforehand, leaving room for a genuine surprise.
AAON_2024q1: AAON entered February 2024 after an exceptionally strong 2023, with the question shifting from operational recovery to whether it could sustain high margins and growth as comparisons got harder and construction softened. Full-year sales had risen over 30% and income over 75%, so investors approached confident rather than skeptical.
AAON_2024q4: AAON entered November 2024 on strong momentum: an exceptional August quarter beat estimates, repairing a weak first-quarter stumble. The bigger catalyst came in October, when AAON disclosed roughly $174.5 million in data-center liquid-cooling orders, turning a qualitative pipeline story into a booked one. Shares were already up about 37%.
ABM_2018q1: ABM entered March 2018 after a rough December report that had missed earnings and cut guidance, sending shares down roughly 16%. Investors approached still skeptical about the cost of the GCA acquisition and its 2020 Vision transformation, watching for evidence that integration risk was stabilizing enough to revalue the deal.
ABM_2018q2: ABM entered Q2 2018 with a sharp gap between improving guidance and poor stock performance — shares had lost roughly a third of their value over the year and sat near a 52-week low, even after Q1 raised EPS guidance. The market remained skeptical about GCA costs and wage pressure.
ABM_2018q3: The months before Q3 2018 followed an unusual June combination — an earnings beat paired with lower full-year guidance. Investors had evidence demand was healthy but labor, overtime and integration costs were still eating into profit. The persistent question was portfolio realignment and GCA integration, not a single new event.
ABM_2018q4: ABM entered fiscal Q4 2018 after a year of repeated doubts about whether GCA and the 2020 Vision transformation could deliver enough margin improvement to justify their cost. Year-end results were a credibility test for the full strategic plan, with new bookings watched as forward indicators.
ABM_2019q1: ABM entered Q1 2019 right after a major re-rating — the December report had beaten estimates, declared GCA integration complete, and set strong new guidance, driving a +20% two-day rally. That raised the bar considerably: investors now needed proof the strong year-end narrative could persist.
ABM_2019q2: ABM entered Q2 2019 after a March quarter that had reportedly beaten earnings but still failed to produce a positive stock reaction. Consensus expected further EPS growth, extending a streak of four consecutive beats, but the lingering question was earnings quality — whether margin gains reflected real integration progress.
ABM_2019q3: ABM entered Q3 2019 after a strong prior beat, but analyst estimates had begun softening, revised about 1.5% lower in the month before the report. The market was balancing a good beat history against concern that labor and macro pressure could slow the ongoing transformation story.
ABM_2019q4: ABM entered Q4 2019 after a difficult autumn — Q3 had produced record revenue and a modest beat, yet shares still declined amid broad downward estimate revisions. The question was whether ABM could finish the year strongly enough to show its pricing and labor discipline was working.
ABM_2020q1: ABM entered Q1 2020 with improving momentum after Q4 rebuilt some credibility, but growing coronavirus uncertainty was starting to dominate markets. Exposure looked ambiguous — closures could cut janitorial and aviation work, while heightened cleaning needs could boost demand — though the report landed just before the full shutdown hit.
ABM_2020q2: The months before Q2 2020 were dominated by COVID-19: ABM's services were designated essential, and clients began demanding infection-control work. Traditional activity in aviation and education was collapsing while higher-margin virus-protection work offered a partial offset, making labor flexibility the central question rather than simple revenue decline.
ABM_2020q3: ABM entered Q3 2020 after a powerful June relief rally driven by evidence that higher-margin COVID work and cost flexibility could offset the pandemic's revenue hit. The question shifted from survival to durability — would enhanced cleaning demand persist as facilities stayed partly closed?
ABM_2020q4: ABM entered Q4 2020 with an already-understood pandemic-era model: pressured normal revenue offset by unusually strong margins from virus-protection work and tight labor management. Q3 had delivered EPS growth and over $130 million of operating cash flow despite a 15% revenue decline.
ABM_2021q1: ABM entered fiscal Q1 2021 after a year in which COVID cleaning demand transformed its margin profile; Q4 produced record cash flow, but the market was already questioning whether that could persist as offices reopened. The test was whether temporary demand could convert into a durable service relationship.
ABM_2021q2: ABM entered Q2 2021 after an exceptional quarter in which virus-protection work and labor discipline drove record profit, raising the bar for proof that strength could broaden beyond temporary cleaning demand. The tension was reopening reviving traditional services versus emergency disinfection work fading from the mix.
ABM_2021q3: ABM entered Q3 2021 with a stronger core business plus a major new deal — the $830 million Able Services acquisition announced in August. That reintroduced integration and leverage risk after years digesting GCA, so investors weighed reopening-driven growth against execution risk from a second large acquisition.
ABM_2021q4: ABM entered Q4 2021 with two major shifts underway: the Able Services acquisition and a new ELEVATE transformation program. The market had to price integration costs and financing risk, with consensus already expecting roughly $0.80 EPS — a beat alone wasn't enough without reassurance spending wouldn't eat the benefit.
ABM_2022q1: ABM entered Q1 2022 after a December selloff had already reset expectations around ELEVATE and Able integration costs — investors knew the transformation would be expensive. Russia's invasion of Ukraine added exceptional macro volatility, pushing energy prices sharply higher, a risk for a labor- and fuel-intensive service company.
ABM_2022q2: ABM entered Q2 2022 on a constructive setup — Q1 had produced 9.1% organic growth and raised guidance — but investors worried about growth quality, as COVID disinfection work declined and ELEVATE spending ramped. The question was whether normalized demand could replace pandemic-era profitability without hurting margins.
ABM_2022q3: ABM entered Q3 2022 after a June selloff in which the market rejected a headline earnings beat because EBITDA margin and cash flow deteriorated as pandemic cleaning work normalized. Margin quality, not revenue growth, became the central question, with the stock already punished for mix concerns.
ABM_2022q4: ABM entered fiscal Q4 2022 after two straight quarters where beats failed to produce durable stock gains, as EBITDA margin kept compressing while the business mix shifted from pandemic work toward acquired, lower-margin services. Investors needed proof pricing and cost control could stabilize profitability by year-end.
ABM_2023q1: ABM entered Q1 2023 still digesting a year of acquisition-driven revenue growth against uneven margins — Q4 had modestly beaten estimates yet shares still fell. Consensus expected roughly $0.77 EPS, with the key question being whether labor, interest expense and ELEVATE spending pressure would finally begin to ease.
ABM_2023q2: ABM entered Q2 2023 after a mixed March quarter where EPS beat but revenue missed and margins stayed pressured. Focus centered on whether pricing and cost control could offset labor and interest expense, while the RavenVolt acquisition offered a potential mix improvement if higher-value projects grew faster.
ABM_2023q3: ABM entered Q3 2023 after a June quarter that finally delivered the margin improvement investors wanted, with EBITDA margin and cash flow both rising. That raised the bar for September, even though shares remained down roughly 13% year-to-date, suggesting the market stayed cautious despite the improvement.
ABM_2023q4: ABM entered Q4 2023 after one of its worst reactions in the dataset — shares fell sharply in September following an EPS miss and a cut to the top end of guidance. December became a credibility test for whether that deterioration was temporary, with consensus around $0.92 EPS.
ABM_2024q1: ABM entered Q1 2024 after a strong December rebound in which earnings, margins, cash flow and capital return all improved. The question shifted again — could ABM sustain that recovery while still funding ELEVATE and technology investments, given the stock had already responded positively to the prior beat?
ABM_2024q2: ABM entered Q2 2024 with improving stock momentum — a rising relative-strength rating and a constructive technical pattern followed a March quarter with 9% earnings growth. Expectations were no longer depressed, so the key issue remained margin: Q1 beat estimates yet EBITDA margin declined on technology and interest costs.
ABM_2024q3: ABM entered Q3 2024 after a strong June reaction, another guidance raise and improved cash generation, setting a higher bar for September. Investors increasingly wanted proof that promised margin expansion would arrive, while the newly announced $119 million Quality Uptime Services acquisition added a fresh integration consideration.
ABM_2024q4: ABM entered fiscal Q4 2024 after a September quarter that beat on EPS and revenue but still failed to produce a durable stock gain, reinforcing the market's focus on margin and cash-flow quality over headline beats. Investors wanted proof Technical Solutions and data-center exposure could lift profitability.
ABSI_2022q3: Absci entered August 2022 from a very depressed stock base — shares had lost roughly three-quarters of their value that year. Despite an early-stage biotech's typical cash burn, the company added momentum: a seven-program antibody-drug-conjugate collaboration in July, plus ongoing Merck and NVIDIA partnerships and a new NY AI lab.
ACCO_2019q3: ACCO entered July 2019 waiting for proof that pricing and consumer diversification could offset tariffs and weak legacy office demand. Recent moves included launching the TruSens air-purifier brand alongside Kensington. The key question was whether back-to-school demand and price increases would translate into stronger operating income for the full year.
ACCO_2019q4: ACCO entered October 2019 after a very strong July reaction — record sales, better margins, higher guidance. During the window it acquired Brazil-based Foroni for about $57 million and authorized $100 million more in buybacks. With the bar raised, Q3 needed to prove margins could hold as seasonal mix normalized.
ACCO_2020q1: ACCO entered February 2020 after a sharp negative reaction to Q3, which showed weaker margins, lower adjusted EPS and unfavorable mix despite record free cash flow. EMEA sales were down 5.9% for the year, softening mid-year before stabilizing. Expectations were low, centered on whether earnings growth could re-establish itself.
ACCO_2021q1: The months before February 2021 were dominated by COVID: legacy office and school demand stayed depressed while Kensington, air purifiers and home-use products benefited from remote work. ACCO also acquired gaming-accessories maker PowerA in December 2020, adding a faster-growth consumer category but also new leverage and integration risk to weigh.
ACCO_2021q2: ACCO entered Q1 2021 with a split narrative: February had shown severe COVID damage to legacy office demand, but newly acquired PowerA offered a faster-growing consumer/gaming platform and EMEA showed relative resilience. Investors wanted proof PowerA's growth and integration justified its price, and that e-commerce categories could keep growing.
ACCO_2022q1: ACCO entered Q4 2021 after a year of strong reopening and PowerA momentum, with the earlier report showing PowerA outperforming. The market wanted to know if those gains could persist as demand normalized and cost inflation intensified. Consensus sat near $0.48 EPS, with the stock down over the prior year.
ACCO_2022q2: ACCO entered Q1 2022 with strong momentum after management forecast another record year, backed by PowerA and reopening demand plus a strong Q4 reaction. The emerging risk was no longer demand but whether inflation, logistics and raw-material costs would outrun pricing actions supporting the already-guided full-year earnings growth.
ACCO_2023q1: ACCO entered February 2023 after a harder second half of 2022 than expected, as inflation, FX and retailer destocking hurt gaming and North American profit. Full-year EPS guidance had been cut materially during the year, leaving investors with low confidence in visibility and a preference for conservative guidance.
ACCO_2023q2: ACCO entered Q1 2023 on low expectations after February showed falling sales, a small EPS miss and weak retailer/gaming demand, with 2023 guidance leaning on price realization, lower freight costs and restructuring. Investors were no longer rewarding revenue growth alone — they wanted proof those margin self-help levers were working.
ACCO_2024q1: ACCO entered Q4 2023 after a year of margin and cash-flow repair despite weak destocking-driven demand and slow office return. Shares had already risen roughly 25% over three months, and a late-January restructuring plan targeting $60 million in annual savings raised the bar for guidance to show savings outpacing pressure.
